source_text: Sit nunc, benedicti, carcer etiam christianis molestus? Vocati sumus ad militiam Dei vivi jam tunc, cum in sacramenti verba respondimus. Nemo miles ad bellum cum deliciis venit; nec de cubiculo ad aciem procedit, sed de papilionibus expeditis et substrictis, ubi omnis duritia et imbonitas et insuavitas constitit. Etiam in pace, labore et incommodis bellum pati jam ediscunt, in armis deambulando, campum decurrendo, fossam moliendo, testudinem densando. Sudore omnia constant, ne corpora atque animi expavescant: de umbra ad solem, de sole ad coelum de tunica ad loricam, de silentio ad clamorem, de quiete ad tumultum. Proinde vos, benedicti, quodcumque hoc durum est, ad exercitationem virtutum animi et corporis deputate. Bonum agonem subituri estis in quo agonothetes, Deus vivus est; xystarches, Spiritus sanctus corona, aeternitatis; brabium, angelicae substantiae, politia in coelis, gloria in saecula saeculorum. Itaque Epistates vester Christus Jesus, qui vos spiritu unxit, et ad hoc scamma produxit, voluit vos ante diem agonis ad duriorem tractationem a liberiore conditione seponere, ut vires corroborarentur in vobis. Nempe enim et athletae segregantur ad strictiorem disciplinam, ut robori aedificando vacent: continentur a luxuria, a cibis laetioribus, a potu jucundiore. Coguntur, cruciantur, fatigantur: quanto plus in exercitationibus laboraverint, tanto plus de victoria sperant. Et illi, inquit Apostolus, ut coronam corruptibilem consequantur; nos aeternam consecuturi. Carcerem nobis pro palaestra interpretemur, ut ad stadium tribunalis bene exercitati incommodis omnibus producamur: quia virtus duritia extruitur, mollitia vero destruitur.
pass_a_gloss: Is now, blessed ones, even prison troublesome to Christians? We were called to the military service of the living God already then, when we responded to the words of the sacrament. No soldier comes to war with luxuries; nor does he proceed to battle from his bedroom, but from tents that are stripped and packed up, where all harshness and unpleasantness and disagreeableness reside. Even in peacetime, they already learn to endure the hardships and troubles of war by marching with arms, running through the field, building a trench, and forming a testudo. They persevere through everything with sweat, so that their bodies and minds do not become frightened: from shade to sun, from sun to heaven, from tunic to armor, from silence to shout, from quiet to tumult. Therefore, you, blessed ones, consider whatever is hard in this to be exercise for the virtues of the soul and body. You are about to undergo a good contest in which the judge is the living God; the master of the contest, the Holy Spirit; the crown, the substance of the angels, citizenship in heaven, glory in the ages of ages. And so your Master, Christ Jesus, who anointed you with spirit and led you to this stage, wanted you to be separated from a freer condition to a harsher treatment before the day of contest, so that your strengths might be confirmed in you. For even athletes are separated to a stricter discipline, so that they may devote themselves to building up their strength: they are restrained from luxury, from more pleasant food, from more enjoyable drink. They are forced, tormented, wearied: the more they labor in exercises, the more they hope for victory. And those, says the Apostle, in order to obtain a corruptible crown; we, an eternal one. Let us interpret prison as a place of exercise, so that we, well-trained by all hardships, may be led to the stadium of the tribunal: because virtue is built up by harshness, but destroyed by softness.

pass_b_english: Is prison now, blessed ones, even a bother to Christians? We were called to the military service of the living God at the very moment we answered the words of the sacrament. No soldier goes to war dragging luxuries; he does not march to the line from a bedroom, but from stripped‑down, packed‑up tents where every harshness, unpleasantness, and disagreeableness lives. Even in peacetime they already learn to endure the hardships and troubles of war — marching under arms, running the field, digging trenches, locking shields in a testudo. They push through everything with sweat so their bodies and minds will not flinch: from shade into sun, from sun into heaven, from tunic into armor, from silence into shouting, from quiet into tumult. Therefore, you blessed ones, treat whatever is hard in this as training for the virtues of soul and body. You are about to enter a noble contest whose judge is the living God, whose master of the games is the Holy Spirit, and whose prize is the substance of angels, citizenship in heaven, glory for ages of ages (2 Timothy 4:8). And so your Master, Christ Jesus, who anointed you with the Spirit and brought you to this arena, chose to pull you from a freer condition into harsher treatment before the day of the contest, so that your strength might be confirmed in you. For even athletes are set apart for stricter discipline so they can devote themselves to building power: they are denied luxury, richer food, more pleasant drink. They are forced, tormented, wearied: the more they labor in training, the more they hope for victory. And those, says the Apostle, do it to win a perishable crown; we, to win an imperishable one. Let us treat prison as our gymnasium, so that, well‑exercised by every hardship, we may be led into the stadium of the tribunal: because virtue is built by harshness and destroyed by softness.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the Latin text. Pass B correctly identifies the allusion to 1 Corinthians 9:25 (noted as 2 Timothy 4:8 in the provided metadata, but the translator correctly identifies the content of the Apostle's quote regarding the corruptible/imperishable crown) and provides a faithful rendering of the technical athletic terms (agonothetes, xystarches, brabium, Epistates).
